title: The Extra Step in the Recipe
passage:
In a home economics class, students were asked to make vegetable soup from the same basic recipe. The instructions listed ingredients, amounts, and cooking times. Most groups followed the steps exactly. One group, however, added an extra step: they tasted the soup before adding the final amount of salt. Their soup needed less salt than the recipe suggested because the stock they had used was already salty.

The teacher used the example to begin a discussion about instructions. A recipe is designed to make a result more reliable, but ingredients are not always identical. Tomatoes can be sweeter or more sour, onions can vary in size, and different brands of stock contain different amounts of salt. Following instructions carefully is important, but so is checking what is actually happening.

The next week, the class repeated the soup lesson with one change. Each group received vegetables of slightly different sizes. Students had to decide whether the written cooking time still made sense. One group cut large carrots into smaller pieces so they would cook at the same speed as potatoes. Another group kept the pieces large and simply cooked them longer. Both approaches worked.

The lesson was not meant to encourage students to ignore recipes. Beginners often need clear instructions because they do not yet know which changes are safe. The teacher explained that flexibility should grow from observation, not random guessing. A student who changes five things at once may not understand why the result improves or becomes worse.

Students wrote notes beside the recipe: ‘taste before final salt,’ ‘check vegetable softness,’ and ‘change one thing at a time.’ These notes turned a fixed set of instructions into a guide that included moments for judgment.

By the end of the unit, many students saw recipes differently. A recipe was not a command that removed the need to think. It was a tested starting point. The extra step of tasting the soup was small, but it represented an important skill: using a plan while still paying attention to the real situation. The same idea could apply beyond cooking. Instructions are most useful when people understand both when to follow them closely and when evidence shows that a careful adjustment is needed.
translation:
家庭科の授業で、生徒たちは同じ基本レシピを使って野菜スープを作りました。材料、量、加熱時間が示され、多くの班がその通りに進めました。ところが一つの班だけ、最後の塩を入れる前に味見をしました。使ったスープストック自体に塩分が多かったため、レシピより少ない塩で十分でした。

先生はこの例から『手順』について話しました。レシピは結果を安定させるためのものですが、材料はいつも同じではありません。トマトの甘さや酸味、玉ねぎの大きさ、スープストックの塩分は変わります。指示を丁寧に守ることも大切ですが、実際に何が起きているか確かめることも必要です。

翌週、少しずつ大きさの違う野菜を各班へ配り、記載された加熱時間がそのまま使えるか考えさせました。大きいニンジンを小さく切る班もあれば、大きいまま長く煮る班もあり、どちらも成功しました。

これはレシピを無視する授業ではありません。初心者には安全で明確な手順が必要です。先生は、柔軟さは適当な思いつきではなく観察から生まれるべきだと説明しました。一度に五つ変えると、何が結果へ影響したのか分かりません。

生徒たちはレシピの横へ『最後の塩の前に味見』『野菜の柔らかさを確認』『変更は一度に一つ』と書き込みました。固定された指示が、判断する場面を含むガイドへ変わりました。

学習の最後、生徒たちはレシピを『考えなくてよい命令』ではなく、『試されてきた出発点』として見るようになりました。味見という小さな一手間は、計画を使いながら現実にも注意を向けるという大切な技能を表しています。この考え方は料理以外にも当てはまります。
